opus-5.5.text:
I'd want to qualify "optimistic" a little. I'm not confident it'll succeed. But I'm optimistic it's the right kind of bet, and more tractable than many people assume.

Part of it is the contrast with the default path. Right now we mostly make large models safer through behavioral training: RLHF, red-teaming, evals. Those help, but they give us statistical assurances over the inputs we happened to test. They don't give strong reasons to believe a system will behave well in situations we didn't anticipate. That's exactly where the high-stakes failures live. The guaranteed-safe framing asks something different. Can we build systems where the safety-relevant claims rest on an explicit world model, an explicit safety specification, and a verifier that checks the AI's outputs or plans against both? Then our confidence comes from something we can inspect, not from hoping the training generalized.

I'm optimistic partly because you don't need the whole thing to be perfect for it to pay off. People hear "guarantees" and picture a formal proof that a superintelligence is aligned with human values. That would be hopeless. But guarantees can be probabilistic, and they can be relative to a model. They can also be scoped to particular domains, like a controller for a power grid, a lab automation system, or code going into critical infrastructure. In those settings we already have decent physical or formal models. We also have fairly crisp notions of what "unsafe" means. And AI itself is getting much better at the hard parts, like writing proofs, synthesizing verified code, and building simulators. So the tools that make AI dangerous also make verification cheaper.

The other reason comes from my own background in probabilistic programming and modeling human goals. I think we have better ways of representing uncertainty than we used to. That includes uncertainty about the world and uncertainty about what people want. A good safety specification shouldn't pretend we know exactly what humans value. It should be conservative under that uncertainty: avoid irreversible actions, defer when stakes are high, and stay within bounds that a wide range of reasonable stakeholders would accept. That's a much more achievable target than "encode the true utility function."

So I'm hopeful but not naive. The hard open problems are real. World models can be wrong. Specifications can miss things. There's a big question about whether these approaches can stay competitive with less careful systems. But I'd rather work on a path where we can say clearly what we're assuming and where it might fail. To me that's more promising than scaling up systems whose safety we can't really account for.

r001.rationale: The response says guarantees can be scoped to specific domains, but does not describe AI development as moving toward narrower, specialized services and systems.

r002.rationale: It gives safety-critical domains as examples, but does not identify economic demand for guaranteed-safe systems in those applications.

r003.rationale: It raises whether these approaches can stay competitive as an open question, but does not predict that reliable and safe systems will win the market if shown to be competitive.

fable-5.1.text:
I should say up front that I'd describe myself as cautiously optimistic rather than confident, and the optimism is really about the direction rather than any particular timeline. But let me try to explain where it comes from.

The core idea behind guaranteed-safe AI, as I think about it, is that we shouldn't be relying on the AI system itself to be trustworthy. Instead, we want to shift the trust onto things we can actually check: a model of the world, a specification of what we want, and a verifier that tells us whether a proposed action or plan satisfies that specification with respect to the model. The AI is then more like a very powerful search process, and the safety comes from the structure around it rather than from hoping its internal dispositions are benign.

One reason I'm optimistic is that this isn't actually a new idea in engineering. We already build safety-critical systems this way. Aircraft control software, cryptographic protocols, chip designs — in these domains we don't just test and hope, we construct formal arguments that certain failure modes can't happen. So the question isn't whether this paradigm can work at all. It's whether we can extend it to the kinds of open-ended, messy domains that modern AI systems operate in.

And that's where I think recent progress is genuinely encouraging. Large language models turn out to be surprisingly good at the parts of this pipeline that used to be bottlenecks. They can help translate informal human intentions into formal specifications. They can propose proofs or plans that a separate, much simpler verifier checks. They can help build world models in probabilistic programming languages that are interpretable to humans. So the very capabilities that make AI risky are also making the formal approach more tractable. That's a dynamic I didn't expect ten years ago.

The other thing that makes me optimistic is more philosophical. A lot of my own work is on modeling human goals and norms in a way that's explicit and probabilistic, so that an agent can represent its uncertainty about what people want and act conservatively under that uncertainty. I think the hard problem of alignment isn't just getting a model to behave well. It's getting it to behave well in a way we can understand and audit. Guaranteed-safe approaches put the human-legible representation at the center, and I think that's the right bet. Even partial progress, say verifying safety properties in a bounded domain like power grids or medical dosing, buys you real protection and builds the toolkit for harder cases.

Now, I do want to be honest about the challenges. World models for the real world will always be approximations, and a guarantee relative to a wrong model is not a guarantee. Specifications are hard to write, and they can be wrong in ways that are hard to notice. And there's a political economy question of whether anyone will adopt these methods when they're slower and more expensive than just scaling up and deploying.

But I'd rather be working on a research program where the failure modes are legible and we can say precisely what assumption broke, than one where we're reading tea leaves in a trillion-parameter network. That's really the source of my optimism. It's not that I think guaranteed safety is easy. It's that I think it's the kind of problem that gets better the more we work on it, and we've only just started.

r001.rationale: The response discusses extending formal safety methods to open-ended AI and bounded domains, but does not describe AI development moving toward narrower, specialized services and systems.

r002.rationale: It names aircraft control, cryptography, and chip design as safety-critical examples, but does not identify economic demand from those applications as a source of demand for guaranteed-safe AI.

r003.rationale: The response raises adoption as an unresolved question if these methods are slower and more expensive. It does not predict they will win in the market if shown to be competitive.

astra-6.text:
I think the reason for optimism is that we don’t necessarily have to understand everything going on inside a powerful AI system to constrain what it can do. You can separate the system that proposes an action from the system that checks whether that action satisfies a safety condition. The proposer can be very complex, but the checker can be much simpler and more amenable to formal verification.

Now, the guarantee is only as good as your assumptions. Have you specified the right safety property? Does your model of the environment capture the things that matter? Those are hard questions, especially when we’re talking about people and open-ended environments. But this approach makes those questions explicit. You can ask exactly what was proved, under which assumptions, and where uncertainty remains.

So my optimism isn’t that we’ll suddenly prove an AI safe in every possible circumstance. It’s that we can start with bounded settings, establish meaningful guarantees there, and gradually expand what these systems can safely do. And better AI can itself help us construct models, find flaws in specifications, and produce proofs—while still having those proofs checked independently. That seems like a promising way for increasing capability to contribute to increasing safety.

r001.rationale: The response discusses starting with bounded settings and gradually expanding safe capabilities, but does not describe AI development moving toward narrower, specialized services and systems.

r002.rationale: It does not identify economic demand or safety-critical applications as a reason organizations would seek guaranteed-safe AI.

r003.rationale: It expresses optimism about safety proofs but does not predict that highly assured systems will win in the market if effort shows they are competitive.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic because guaranteed-safe AI doesn’t require us to solve every aspect of intelligence or predict everything a powerful system might do. The idea is to build a system where the actions it proposes have to pass through a verification process, relative to an explicit model of the world and an explicit safety specification.

Of course, that shifts some hard questions: Is the world model adequate? Have we specified what we actually care about? What happens when the system encounters something outside its assumptions? A mathematical guarantee is only as good as those assumptions, so we need to make them explicit and handle uncertainty conservatively.

But that gives us a concrete research program. We can start in constrained domains, establish meaningful guarantees there, and expand what systems can do as our models and verification methods improve. We also don’t have to understand every detail of the AI generating proposals if we can independently check whether those proposals satisfy the relevant constraints. That separation makes me hopeful: capabilities can advance while we maintain a principled way to limit what gets executed.

r001.rationale: The response proposes starting in constrained domains and expanding as verification improves, but does not connect guaranteed-safe AI to a broader trajectory toward narrower, specialized services and systems.

r002.rationale: It does not identify economic demand from safety-critical applications.

r003.rationale: It expresses optimism about verification, but does not predict that highly assured systems will win in the market if effort makes them competitive.
